title: JavaScript Origins: Mocha, LiveScript and the JavaScript Name
learningObjectives: Describe the creation of JavaScript at Netscape in the mid-1990s.
Identify Brendan Eich as the language's original creator and Netscape as its initial development environment.
Explain that Mocha and LiveScript were early names used during the language's development and release period.
Describe how the name JavaScript became associated with the language without implying that it is a version of Java.
Explain why the language name and the ECMAScript standard name are related but not identical historical terms.
Distinguish a historical marketing name from the language's technical design and standardization.
Recognize that modern JavaScript implementations are based on the ECMAScript specification.
Explain why early browser scripting focused on responding to user actions and making pages interactive.
Use reliable historical references when describing dates, names and people connected with language history.
Summarize JavaScript's origin without confusing its history with Java or later runtime environments.

understand.concept: JavaScript was created at Netscape in the mid-1990s by Brendan Eich for use in the browser. During its early development it was known by the working name Mocha, then LiveScript, before the name JavaScript was used for the browser release. The name's similarity to Java was a historical naming and marketing choice; the languages are distinct. JavaScript later became standardized as ECMAScript.
understand.whyItMatters: Knowing the origin of JavaScript helps explain its browser-first beginnings and clears up common confusion about Java. It also shows why the language's historical name, its standard specification and the different runtimes that execute it should be treated as related but distinct ideas.
understand.analogy: A product can begin with a working name, receive a release name and later be described by a formal standard. Those labels refer to the same evolving technology in different contexts.
understand.analogyLimit: A name change does not mean a new language was created each time. Mocha, LiveScript and JavaScript refer to stages in the history of the language that became modern JavaScript.
understand.history: TC39's FAQ records the early Mocha and LiveScript names and the later JavaScript name. The first edition of ECMA-262 was adopted in June 1997. Historical details should be stated carefully because naming, beta releases and standardization occurred over a short period and are often simplified in popular summaries.

explain.narrative:
JavaScript was developed at Netscape in 1995 for browser scripting. Brendan Eich created the language, which was initially developed under the working name Mocha. It was later called LiveScript in a Netscape Navigator beta and then JavaScript for its release. These names describe the early naming history of the language, not three separate modern languages that a developer must learn.

The JavaScript name was associated with Java during a period when Java was receiving substantial attention. Despite the similar names, JavaScript and Java have different language designs, type systems, runtimes and ecosystems. JavaScript is not a subset of Java and Java is not required to write JavaScript.

As the language spread beyond one browser vendor, a shared specification became important. ECMA-262 was adopted in 1997 under the name ECMAScript. JavaScript remains the familiar name used for the language in browsers and runtimes, while ECMAScript identifies the standardized core language specification.

Historical names are useful context, but modern development should focus on the language and platform features supported by the target runtime. When publishing a timeline, distinguish the language's creation, its early naming stages and the later standardization process.

examples.title: A simplified early naming timeline
examples.code:
Netscape, 1995
  → early working name: Mocha
  → beta-era name: LiveScript
  → release name: JavaScript

ECMA-262 first edition adopted: June 1997
Standardized language name: ECMAScript
examples.explanation: The names describe the history of one evolving language. ECMAScript became the formal standard name, while JavaScript remained the common product and developer-facing name.
examples.expectedOutput: You can order the early names and explain the relationship to ECMAScript.

examples.title: Java and JavaScript are not the same language
examples.explanation: The examples use different syntax and execution environments. Similar names do not mean the languages share one runtime or one source-code format.
examples.expectedOutput: Both examples print Hello in their respective environments, but they are written in different languages.

examples.title: JavaScript and ECMAScript terminology
examples.code:
JavaScript = familiar name of the language
ECMAScript = standardized core language specification
Browser APIs = host capabilities such as DOM and Fetch
Runtime = environment that executes code and exposes host services
examples.explanation: The names are related but refer to different layers. A browser JavaScript program may use both ECMAScript features and Web APIs.
examples.expectedOutput: You can distinguish the language name, its standard and the browser environment.
